newsitem.title: CONGO: Brazzaville peace moves falter, fighting picks up.
newsitem.headline: Brazzaville peace moves falter, fighting picks up.

text.p: Fighting flared in Congo's capital Brazzaville on Thursday as a ceasefire designed to halt a week of bloody clashes between supporters of President Pascal Lissouba and his predecessor failed to take hold.

The city centre echoed to automatic gunfire, punctuated by explosions of mortars and rocket-propelled grenades, one day after broadcast truce calls from Lissouba and former Marxist military leader Denis Sassou Nguesso.
Near the French and U.S. embassies, large numbers of government troops took cover in deep drainage channels and fired towards positions held by Sassou Nguesso's Cobra militia.

"The ceasefire has not be totally followed. That's clear. There have been shots," Brazzaville Mayor Bernard Kolelas, who negotiated the truce calls, told Reuters during a break in a meeting of his mediation committee.
Kolelas's Ninja militia took part in fighting which killed 2,000 people in Brazzaville in 1993 and 1994 after a disputed parliamentary poll. They have not been involved this time.
Western military sources said battle lines remained static in the city centre but the Cobras were advancing in the suburbs towards the zoo, along one of the roads towards the airport.

But French army officials at the airport said things seemed calmer than early in the conflict, which began when soldiers surrounded Sassou Nguesso's home as part of a crackdown on private militias before a July 27 presidential election.

French military spokesman Colonel Henry Pelissier said France had 1,200 troops on the ground and that they had evacuated more than 3,000 foreign nationals. He estimated that a further 500 Western nationals might still need evacuating.
But he played down talk of any French intervention.

"The only mission we have at the moment is to protect and transport foreigners...We don't have a defence accord with Congo and I don't see why at this stage we should put ourselves in the middle as a buffer force," Pelissier said.

Congolese army spokesman Colonel Jean-Marie Ompebe said: "Sadly the ceasefire does not seem to be very much respected. We have tried to respect it but if they fire then our men fire back. Sometimes soldiers from both sides just open fire because they are nervous."
At the French army base near the airport hundreds of foreign civilians, most of them West Africans, awaited evacuation and cowered as shells landed only 200 metres (yards) away.
"We prefer not to keep civilians here because we have the two sides firing at other across the airport and across us," Pelissier said, drawing lines in the dust to show different positions.
A French soldier was wounded just above the knee. Pelissier said this did not look like a deliberate provocation.
A red-eyed Sassou Nguesso fighter, Mbongo Dafoa, 17, a bandanna round his head, said: "We are fighting to take power from the tribalist Lissouba. We are going to take power by any means."
Across the road from the U.S. embassy a soldier struggled under the weight of electronic goods looted from a nearby store.
In the city centre, the body of a boy lay on the roadside in an area controlled by Sassou Nguesso's forces. Blood flowed from his head. His school bag was on his back.
Bodies lay in other streets. Aid workers and military officials have not reached all areas to compile a death toll.

Lissouba won a 1992 presidential election after Sassou Nguesso, president from 1979, bowed to calls for multi-party politics. Lissouba defeated Kolelas in a runoff after Sassou Nguesso was knocked out in the first round.
